report:
Based on the evidence, your skepticism is largely justified, though the picture is nuanced rather than flatly "false."

**What the research shows:**

A comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (Whigham et al., published via Springer) found that long-term CLA supplementation produces only a small, statistically significant reduction in body fat—averaging roughly 0.05–0.1 kg/week, amounting to about 0.1 kg/week of fat loss over time. The effect, while statistically detectable, is modest and of doubtful practical or clinical significance (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00394-011-0253-9).

A more recent systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis in the *British Journal of Nutrition* similarly evaluated CLA's effects on body composition markers including waist circumference, fat mass, and body fat percentage across RCTs, generally confirming small effect sizes rather than robust abdominal-fat-specific reductions (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/effects-of-conjugated-linoleic-acid-supplementation-on-anthropometrics-and-body-composition-indices-in-adults-a-systematic-review-and-doseresponse-metaanalysis/A3F12F07BB3118D4F757D901C6E1E366).

Some individual trials, such as one in obese, middle-aged men with metabolic syndrome features, did report reduced abdominal adipose tissue specifically (via Frontiers in Nutrition), but such positive findings are inconsistent across the literature and often come from smaller or shorter studies (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2024.1336889/full).

Reviews on CLA's broader physiological effects (PMC) also note concerns about insulin resistance and metabolic side effects, particularly with the trans-10,cis-12 isomer, further undermining CLA's viability as a safe, effective fat-loss aid (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6413010/).

**Conclusion:** The claim that CLA supplements meaningfully reduce abdominal fat is not well supported. Evidence shows only small, inconsistent effects that lack clear clinical relevance, with some safety concerns—supporting a "mostly false" or "overstated" verdict rather than a robust health benefit.
